title: “COME TO ME”—THE THREE WORDS EXHAUSTED CHRISTIANS KEEP READING TOO FAST
paragraphs:
“COME TO ME”—THE THREE WORDS EXHAUSTED CHRISTIANS KEEP READING TOO FAST
What Jesus Really Meant by “Come to Me, All Who Are Weary”—and Why His Invitation May Be Speaking to the Part of You That Is Tired of Pretending You’re Fine
There is a kind of tiredness sleep cannot cure.
You can sleep eight hours and wake up carrying it.
You can take a vacation and pack it in your suitcase.
You can sit in church, raise your hands during worship, smile when somebody asks how you are doing, whisper “God is good” at exactly the right moment...
and still go home exhausted.
Not merely physically tired.
Soul tired.
Tired of fighting the same temptation.
Tired of wondering why the prayer still seems unanswered.
Tired of carrying everybody while quietly wondering who would carry you if you finally collapsed.
Tired of trying to be the strong Christian.
Tired of disappointing yourself.
Tired of promising God, “This is the last time,” only to find yourself kneeling beside the wreckage of another failure.
Tired of hiding.
Tired of performing.
Tired of being needed.
Tired of being afraid.
Tired of knowing Bible verses your heart seems too wounded to feel.
And somewhere inside all that exhaustion, there may be a question you are almost afraid to say aloud:
“Jesus... what if I don’t have much left?”
That is exactly why three words spoken by Christ deserve to be heard again.
Not as Christian wall art.
Not as a comforting caption beneath a photograph of a sunset.
Not as religious anesthesia.
Listen to them as though you were standing in the crowd when they first left His mouth.
“Come to Me.”
The Gospel of Matthew preserves the saying in Greek:
“Δεῦτε πρός με πάντες οἱ κοπιῶντες καὶ πεφορτισμένοι, κἀγὼ ἀναπαύσω ὑμᾶς.”
“Come to Me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest.”
Matthew 11:28.
Slow down.
Because the most astonishing part of that sentence may not be “rest.”
It may be “Me.”
Jesus does not merely say, “Come learn a better coping mechanism.”
He does not say, “Come discover the hidden strength already inside yourself.”
He does not say, “Come fix yourself, clean yourself, prove yourself, and then perhaps I will receive you.”
He says:
“Come to Me.”
That changes everything.
The Greek expression begins, “Δεῦτε πρός με”—deute pros me.
“Come to Me.”
It is an invitation toward a Person.
Christianity, at its center, is not exhausted people being handed another religious checklist.
It is sinners being summoned to Christ.
And the context makes this even more breathtaking.
Immediately before this invitation, Jesus speaks about His unique relationship with the Father and declares that the Father is known through the Son. Then comes the invitation.
Come to Me.
In other words, Jesus is not standing on the roadside merely offering inspirational advice to stressed people.
He is placing Himself at the center of the invitation.
The exhausted are summoned to Him.
The burdened are summoned to Him.
And that means your deepest need is not merely a lighter schedule.
You need Jesus.
Maybe that is difficult to hear because we have become experts at treating symptoms.
We think, “If I could just make more money, I would finally breathe.”
“If my marriage changed, I would finally have peace.”
“If this anxiety disappeared...”
“If my children came back...”
“If the diagnosis changed...”
“If people understood me...”
“If I could undo what I did...”
“If I could stop thinking about what they did to me...”
“If God would finally answer this one prayer...”
Then I could rest.
Some of those desires are completely understandable. Some are things worth praying about.
But Jesus goes beneath them.
Because you can have money and still have no rest.
You can have applause and still hate the silence.
You can have thousands of followers and feel completely unseen.
You can escape one difficult season and discover that your own heart traveled with you.
Jesus does not merely offer changed circumstances.
He offers Himself.
And notice who receives the invitation.
“πάντες οἱ κοπιῶντες καὶ πεφορτισμένοι.”
All who are laboring and burdened.
The word translated “weary” or “laboring” comes from κοπιάω, carrying the sense of laboring, working to the point of weariness.
Then Matthew gives us πεφορτισμένοι—a form describing those who have been loaded or burdened.
Do you see the picture?
People exhausted from carrying.
And perhaps that describes somebody reading this right now.
You have become frighteningly good at carrying things nobody knows about.
You carry childhood wounds into adult relationships.
You carry rejection into every room and call it independence.
You carry shame underneath ministry.
You carry pornography underneath worship songs.
You carry resentment underneath politeness.
You carry fear underneath ambition.
You carry loneliness underneath jokes.
You carry disappointment with God underneath theological answers.
You carry secret sin underneath public Christianity.
Nobody sees the weight because you learned how to smile while lifting it.
But Jesus sees.
And He says:
Come.
Not when you have conquered everything.
Come.
Not when you have become impressive.
Come.
Not after you have hidden the evidence.
Come.
There is something scandalous about grace because grace destroys our favorite illusion—that somehow we can make ourselves worthy enough to need less mercy.
The Gospel says something far more humbling and far more beautiful.
You cannot save yourself.

Sin is not merely a collection of unfortunate habits requiring self-improvement. Scripture describes humanity as guilty before God and unable to establish its own righteousness. We have sinned. We need reconciliation. We need forgiveness. We need a Savior.
And Christianity announces that God did not wait for sinners to climb their way back to Him.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He lived in righteousness.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the One saying “Come to Me” is not offering cheap comfort that pretends your sin does not matter.
He is the Savior who dealt with sin at the cost of His own blood.
That is why grace is not God saying your rebellion was insignificant.
Grace is God demonstrating just how serious sin is—and how astonishing His mercy is—at the cross.
Maybe you have spent years thinking Jesus is waiting for the improved version of you.
Read His invitation again.
“Come to Me.”
But now we must keep reading, because this is where one of the most beautiful sayings of Jesus is sometimes misunderstood.
Christ does not say:
“Come to Me, and you will never carry anything again.”
He says:
“Take My yoke upon you.”
That sounds almost shocking.
You came carrying a burden...
and Jesus mentions a yoke?
The Greek reads:
“ἄρατε τὸν ζυγόν μου ἐφ’ ὑμᾶς καὶ μάθετε ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ...”
“Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me...”
Matthew 11:29.
Jesus is not inviting you into autonomous comfort.
He is inviting you into discipleship.
This is not “Jesus will make sure nothing difficult ever happens to you.”
He Himself tells His followers elsewhere that discipleship includes self-denial and a cross.
The apostles suffered.
The early church suffered.
Faithfulness has never meant exemption from pain.
So what kind of rest is this?
Listen to Jesus finish the sentence:
“...καὶ εὑρήσετε ἀνάπαυσιν ταῖς ψυχαῖς ὑμῶν.”
“And you will find rest for your souls.”
Your souls.
This goes deeper than circumstances.
The word ἀνάπαυσις carries the idea of rest, repose, refreshment.
Jesus is speaking to something beneath your calendar.
Beneath your workload.
Beneath your public image.
The soul.
And there is another detail we cannot miss.
Jesus describes Himself.
“πραΰς εἰμι καὶ ταπεινὸς τῇ καρδίᾳ.”
“I am gentle and humble in heart.”
Think about who is saying this.
The One through whom we come to know the Father.
The Lord who commands repentance.
The King before whom every knee will ultimately bow.
And when burdened sinners approach Him, He tells them something about His heart:
Gentle.
Humble.
Some people are afraid to come to Jesus because they have confused Him with the people who misrepresented Him.
Perhaps somebody used Scripture to humiliate you.
Perhaps religion became a place where everybody performed holiness while wounds were pushed underground.
Perhaps you were taught to fear everybody discovering who you really were.
Perhaps you started believing God tolerates you from a distance but secretly wishes you were somebody else.
But listen to Christ describe His own heart.
Gentle.
Humble.
This does not mean indifferent toward sin.
The Jesus who says “Come” also calls people to repentance.
Grace never requires God to pretend darkness is light.
Jesus loves sinners too much to bless the chains destroying them.
He receives us as we come, but His grace does not leave us where sin has taken us.
That is why coming to Christ is both comfort and surrender.
You bring Him the burden.
And you take His yoke.
You stop pretending you are your own savior.
You stop negotiating with the sin you were commanded to forsake.
You stop using grace as permission to remain unchanged.
You stop trying to earn what only mercy can give.
You come.
You repent.
You believe.
You learn from Him.
You follow Him.
And slowly, sometimes painfully, sometimes through tears nobody sees, Christ begins rewriting what sin tried to make the final chapter.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
That would not be redemption.
He enters the wreckage.
Peter denied Him.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
The man who insisted he would remain faithful crumbled when faithfulness became dangerous.
Then came the rooster.
Sometimes one sound can carry an entire lifetime of regret.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
But failure did not get Peter’s final sentence.
The risen Christ restored him.
Not because denial suddenly became acceptable.
Not because Peter deserved another chance.
Grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Think of the woman in John 4.
Complicated history.
Broken relationships.
A life Jesus knew before she explained it.
Yet Christ deliberately met her beside a well and offered living water.
Her history was real.
But her history was not more powerful than the One sitting beside her.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Think about the criminal dying beside Jesus.
No lifetime left to repair his reputation.
No decades available to accumulate religious achievements.
He could not climb down from his cross and build an impressive testimony.
He could only turn toward Christ.
And Christ was enough.
Maybe that is why this invitation frightens us.
Because “Come to Me” means surrendering the fantasy that someday we will save ourselves.
There is a strange exhaustion produced by self-salvation.
Always proving.
Always comparing.
Always hiding.
Always wondering whether you have prayed enough, accomplished enough, suffered enough, given enough, impressed enough people, cleaned yourself thoroughly enough for God to finally want you.
But you cannot outperform your need for grace.
The Gospel does not say, “Try harder until God owes you.”
The Gospel says Christ has done what sinners could never do for themselves.
This does not produce laziness.
Grace produces worship.
Obedience stops being a desperate attempt to purchase God's love and becomes the grateful response of someone who has been loved in Christ.
And maybe tonight, that is the burden beneath all your other burdens.
You are exhausted from trying to be enough.
Enough for your parents.
Enough for your spouse.
Enough for your church.
Enough for the internet.
Enough for yourself.
Maybe even enough for God.
Jesus says:
Come to Me.
You do not need to impress the One who already knows everything.
He knows the thought you never told anyone.
He knows what happened behind that closed door.
He knows the relapse.
He knows the bitterness.
He knows the questions.
He knows the night you nearly gave up.
He knows why you became cold.
He knows why you stopped trusting people.
He knows the prayer you are embarrassed to pray.
He knows.
And still the invitation stands.
Come to Me.
But do not confuse coming with merely feeling emotional while reading Christian words.
Come means come.
Turn toward Christ.
Bring the sin into the light.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Ask for help where secrecy has become your prison.
Open Scripture again.
Pray even when your prayer comes out broken.
Return to fellowship if isolation has been feeding your darkness.
Stop waiting to become worthy of mercy.
You never will.
That is why mercy is mercy.
Perhaps somebody reading this has been away from Jesus for years.
You still know the songs.
You still know when to say “Amen.”
You know enough Christian vocabulary to make everybody believe you are spiritually alive.
But inside?
Dry.
Far away.
Secretly compromised.
Exhausted from pretending.
Maybe you have wondered whether you have gone too far.
Hear the invitation again.
Come to Me.
Not to an internet personality.
Not to Gospel Warrior.
Not to a denomination.
Not to a personality cult.
To Jesus Christ.
Everything we write should ultimately become a finger pointing beyond ourselves toward Him.
Jesus saves.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus restores.
Jesus transforms.
Jesus is Lord.
And if these words have exposed something you have been hiding, do not rush past that moment.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need impressive language.
Maybe it is simply:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
There is no trophy for pretending.
And somebody else reading your comment may finally find the courage to stop pretending too.
Because there may come a night when the strong version of you disappears again.
A night when the old accusation returns.
A night when the burden feels heavier.
Come back and remember:
Jesus never said you had to become invulnerable.
He said you had to come.
Financial support is not what makes someone faithful to Christ, but generous believers have always been able to use their resources to help Gospel ministry go farther.
It is discipleship.
Truth.
Encouragement.
Conviction.
Accountability.
Biblical nourishment.
And helping put the Gospel before another weary human being.
Then invite someone with you.
A struggling believer.
A family member who has drifted.
A friend who quietly stopped praying.
A lukewarm Christian.
A seeker.
Even someone who does not yet believe.
Because somewhere tonight, a person is lying awake believing exhaustion is proof that God has abandoned them.
Somebody is scrolling through Facebook because silence makes the pain louder.
Somebody is hiding a failure.
Somebody is considering giving up.
Somebody thinks their scandal became their identity.
And perhaps God can use something as ordinary as your share to put an extraordinary invitation in front of them:
Come to Me.
Not “fix yourself.”
Come.
Not “pretend harder.”
Come.
Not “hide until you become respectable.”
Come.
To Christ.
And when you come, you discover that the hands receiving weary sinners are the same hands that were pierced for them.
That is where the burden finally meets grace.
At the feet of Jesus.
So if you remember nothing else from these words, remember this:
You were never meant to carry the weight of being your own savior when the Savior Himself is still saying, “Come to Me.”
